Setting up a reptile terrarium in a weekend

Posted on March 3 by Sam

Building a terrarium sounds like a big project, but most of the work is planning. If you know your animal's temperature range, humidity needs and how much it likes to climb, the shopping list almost writes itself.

Start with the enclosure. Glass is easy to clean and holds humidity well; screen enclosures breathe better and suit species from dry, airy habitats. Front-opening doors are worth paying for, since lizards tend to read anything coming from above as a predator.

Heat and light

Reptiles regulate their temperature by moving between warm and cool spots, so you need a gradient, not one even temperature. A basking lamp at one end and nothing at the other is the simplest way to get it.

SpeciesBasking °CHumidity
Veiled chameleon3250–70%
Leopard gecko3330–40%
Crested gecko2660–80%

Use a thermostat on every heat source. Thermometers tell you something has gone wrong; thermostats stop it going wrong in the first place, and they are cheap compared to a vet bill.

The best enclosure is the one you can keep clean without dreading it.

Automating the misting

If you're comfortable with a microcontroller, a humidity sensor and a small pump will keep things steady. Here is the core loop I use:

while (true) {
  if (humidity() < 55) mist(3000);
  sleep(60_000);
}
  • Substrate: coco fibre or bioactive soil
  • Plants: pothos, ficus, bromeliads
  • Water: dripper for chameleons, dish for most others

Give the setup a few days to stabilise before the animal moves in. Watch the readings at different times of day, and adjust the lamp height before you adjust anything else.
